title: The Glorification of Violence in Grappler Baki
summary: Part 3 of NH's Grappler Baki analysis. He argues that violence is the backbone of the series: it builds character through how fighters take and deal pain, it carries a Darwinian survival-of-the-fittest philosophy, and it sets up a subculture where ultraviolence loses its taboo. He uses this to defend martial arts manga against the charge of being brainless.
claims: Violence is part of daily life whether you like it or not, and believing you will never face it is the sign of a childish, unprepared mind
Martial artists accept that violence is inevitable and learn to control their own power; a man who refuses to recognise his power risks having it destroy something he loves
Martial arts series are unfairly seen as brainless; Grappler Baki uses violence to build characters and ideas instead of avoiding writing
Baki characters reveal personality through how they react to pain, such as Jack shrugging off an arm broken in seven places, rather than through dialogue
Pain in Baki is exaggerated but bounded (losing pints of blood is survivable, decapitation is not), which keeps dramatic tension without cheapening outcomes
Baki presents violence as neither good nor evil; it simply exists, and the strong devour the weak
Itagaki uses brutality to criticise the watering down of martial arts, which in the series should be survival of the fittest: martial arts is not sport, it is war
A one-track mind ignores common sense, which is why the sound objections of the series' female voice of reason are always ignored by the fighters
